newsitem.title: ANGOLA: FEATURE - Scarred Angola town hopes peace is here to stay.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Scarred Angola town hopes peace is here to stay.

text.p: The streets of this city are quiet, save for the occasional chatter of a cluster of boys playing soccer or tinny music filtering from one of the few bars.

But Malange's tranquility belies its recent past. Its buildings, like those of so many others in Angola, bear testimony to 20 years of civil war. There is hardly a block without a pockmarked facade or a bombed or burned-out home.
After nearly two years of peace, life has improved markedly. But Angola has encountered false dawns before and people are still wary of any promises of a secure future.

This week, Angola's former foes together with the United Nations and three observer countries monitoring the peace process agreed that sufficient progress was being made to permit the start of a U.N. withdrawal of peacekeepers.
The first units will be leaving shortly, and the entire force of 6,500 men could be out by next February.

But people in Malange are still not completely convinced that the rival UNITA (National Unity for the Total Independence of Angola) and MPLA (Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola) will be truly reconciled.

In October, UNITA leader Jonas Savimbi refused to take up his designated post as a vice president serving under MPLA president Jose Eduardo dos Santos. He refused to come to the capital when U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher stopped over in Luanda to try to nudge Angola forward.

While the United Nations has seen steady progress since then on the business of demilitarisation, little political headway has been made. Earlier this month, the Luanda government unilaterally extended parliament's mandate for two years, prompting complaints from UNITA that they were not consulted.
Danger to peace also lurks in Angola's vast, remote diamond region where there are enough riches literally lying around to ignite fresh rows over who gets what.
The civil war in the former Portuguese colony was especially vicious to Malange, a city held by the government but long surrounded by UNITA rebels.

As recently as November 1993, residents were dying at the rate of over 250 a day during a siege by UNITA that lasted for two years. At one point aid groups were flying in some 140 tonnes of food a day.
Now, life is slowly returning to normal. People are working, businesses are open with goods to sell, and farmers are planting their crops.
But even though Malange seems on the mend, its people are thoroughly pessimistic about the continuation of the recovery and seem to prepare themselves daily for a return to bad times.

"You can walk around town these days and see children playing in the streets, more businesses opening up and farmers working the fields," said Lidia Fortunato, an Angolan working for an aid agency in Malange.

"But there is still a deep sense of scepticism about things continuing this way, about the peace process in general. People here have suffered a lot and have been told there would be peace before and now they just don't believe it anymore."
For a short time in 1992 it looked as though peace might reign after elections were held under U.N. supervision and the ruling MPLA returned to power with a democratic majority.

But Savimbi refused to accept defeat at the polls and took his soldiers back to the bush. Renewed fighting broke out and would continue until the two sides signed peace accords in the Zambian capital Lusaka in November 1994.

The situation in Malange, a pretty site in the lush central highlands, has improved vastly since the days of the siege. Statistics from the Irish aid organisation Concern show malnutrition rates have fallen from 34 percent in November 1994 to about four percent in July 1996.
General food distribution ceased months ago. Now most buy food at the central market or grow crops on the city outskirts.
Most aid groups have shifted gears from emergency work to long-term development, while some see an end to their work in the area in the not too distant future.
"I think with two good harvests we can close our office here," said Jean-Charles Dei, director of the World Food Programme in Malange.
The fresh fruits and vegetables that flow into Malange every day come from surrounding UNITA-controlled areas.
On a recent morning on the road east into UNITA territory, residents of Malange carried soap, fuel, salt and goods bought at local stores to trade with farmers for fresh produce.
"All of this comes from the UNITA zones," said a woman at Malange's central market, gesturing at stacks of potatoes and papayas spread out at her pitch.
The stalls around her, empty not long ago, overflowed with mangoes, bananas, potatoes, coffee and canned goods.
But when asked about the future, she only shrugged and said she could not think about tomorrow because the government or UNITA might decide any time to go back to war.
The country has huge economic potential, with vast diamond deposits, rich oilfields, abundant agricultural land and untapped mineral wealth.
Southern Africa, no longer dissected by the anti-apartheid frontiers around South Africa, is poised for an era of open trading and rising international investment.

Another recent visitor to Angola was International Monetary Fund Managing Director Michel Camdessus, who authorised a $75 million emergency programme to help rebuild the shattered economy and finance the integration of its formerly warring armies into a national unity force.

News of Camdessus's visit did not make much impact on the people of Malange. They do not need to be told at this point that renewed confrontation would frighten off aid, investors and world sympathy, reducing them back to the misery they have only recently escaped.
